Content:
A binomial distribution is a probability distribution that models the number of successes in a sequence of [MATH: n] independent experiments (or trials) where each outcome is either success or failure. In a binomial distribution, the probability of success in each experiment is the same.

Content:
If there are [MATH: n] experiments and [MATH: p] is the probability of success on each experiment, then the number of successes has the following probability mass function:

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \qquad x=0,1,2, \ldots, n]

Content:
For example, if we flip a coin [MATH: 5] times, then the number of heads follows a binomial distribution.

Content:
- Each toss is an experiment that either results in success (i.e., heads) or failure (i.e., tails).
- There are [MATH: n=5] experiments.
- Each experiment has a probability [MATH: p=\dfrac{1}{2}] of success.

Content:
So, the number of heads has the following probability mass function:

Content:
[MATH: f(x)|= ((5)/(x))((1)/(2))^{x}(1 − (1)/(2))^{5 − x}; = ((5)/(x))((1)/(2))^{x}((1)/(2))^{5 − x}; = ((5)/(x))((1)/(2))^{5}]

Content:
When a random variable [MATH: X] follows a binomial distribution consisting of [MATH: n] experiments (or trials) and the probability of success on each trial is [MATH: p,] we often write

Content:
[MATH: X\sim B(n,p).]

Content:
In words, we say, "the random variable [MATH: X] follows a binomial distribution with [MATH: n] trials and probability [MATH: p] of success on each trial."

sections.normalized_html: It is known that [MATH: 75\%] of students pass a particular exam. If [MATH: 5] students who took the exam are randomly selected, what is the probability that [MATH: 3] of them passed the exam? Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.
sections.readable_text: It is known that [MATH: 75\%] of students pass a particular exam. If [MATH: 5] students who took the exam are randomly selected, what is the probability that [MATH: 3] of them passed the exam? Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let the random variable [MATH: X] be equal to the number of students that passed the exam.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are [MATH: n=5] students

  • the probability that each student passed the exam is [MATH: p=75\%=0.75]

So, [MATH: X] follows a binomial distribution, where [MATH: X\sim B(5,0.75).] We want to find the probability that [MATH: x=3] of the students passed the exam.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

[MATH: P(X=x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x},]

where [MATH: n] is the number of experiments, and [MATH: p] is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

[MATH: P(X = 3)|= ((5)/(3))(0.75)^{3}(1 − 0.75)^{5 − 3}; = (5!)/(3!(5 − 3)!)(0.75)^{3}(0.25)^{2}; = 10(0.75)^{3}(0.25)^{2}; = 0.264]

rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html: A standard fair die is rolled [MATH: 8] times. What is the probability of rolling an even number at least [MATH: 7] times? Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.
sections.readable_text: A standard fair die is rolled [MATH: 8] times. What is the probability of rolling an even number at least [MATH: 7] times? Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let the random variable [MATH: X] be equal to the number of times we get an even number.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are [MATH: n=8] rolls

  • the probability of rolling an even number on any roll of the die is [MATH: p=\dfrac{3}{6} = 0.5]

So, [MATH: X] follows a binomial distribution, where [MATH: X\sim B(8,0.5).]

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

[MATH: P(X=x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x},]

where [MATH: n] is the number of experiments, and [MATH: p] is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

[MATH: P(X = x)|= ((8)/(x))(0.5)^{x}(1 − 0.5)^{8 − x}; = ((8)/(x))(0.5)^{x}(0.5)^{8 − x}.]

We want to find the probability of rolling an even number at least [MATH: 7] times. So, we compute

[MATH: P(X ≥ 7)|= P(X = 7) + P(X = 8); = ((8)/(7))(0.5)^{7}(0.5)^{8 − 7} + ((8)/(8))(0.5)^{8}(0.5)^{8 − 8}; = 8(0.5)^{7}(0.5) + 1(0.5)^{8}; = 0.035]

rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let the random variable [MATH: X] be equal to the number of games that the player wins.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are [MATH: n=12] games

  • the probability of winning each game is [MATH: p=40\%=0.4]

So, [MATH: X] follows a binomial distribution, where [MATH: X\sim B(12,0.4).]

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

[MATH: P(X=x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x},]

where [MATH: n] is the number of experiments, and [MATH: p] is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

[MATH: P(X = x)|= ((12)/(x))(0.4)^{x}(1 − 0.4)^{12 − x}; = ((12)/(x))(0.4)^{x}(0.6)^{12 − x}.]

We want to find the probability that the player wins at least 2 of the games. This corresponds to [MATH: P(X \geq 2).]

However, computing

[MATH: P(X \geq 2) = P(X=2) + P(X=3) + \ldots + P(X=12)]

will involve many computations, so let's express our answer in terms of the complement instead. By doing this, we get

[MATH: P(X ≥ 2)|= 1 − P(X < 2); = 1 − [P(X = 0) + P(X = 1)]; = 1 − [((12)/(0))(0.4)^{0}(0.6)^{12 − 0} + ((12)/(1))(0.4)^{1}(0.6)^{12 − 1}]; = 1 − [(0.6)^{12} + 12(0.4)(0.6)^{11}]; = 1 − 0.019591; = 0.980]

rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A binomial distribution is a probability distribution that models the number of successes in a sequence of [MATH: n] independent experiments (or trials) where each outcome is either success or failure. In a binomial distribution, the probability of success in each experiment is the same.

Content:
If there are [MATH: n] experiments and [MATH: p] is the probability of success on each experiment, then the number of successes has the following probability mass function:

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}, \qquad x=0,1,2, \ldots, n]

Content:
For example, if we flip a coin [MATH: 5] times, then the number of heads follows a binomial distribution.

Content:
- Each toss is an experiment that either results in success (i.e., heads) or failure (i.e., tails).
- There are [MATH: n=5] experiments.
- Each experiment has a probability [MATH: p=\dfrac{1}{2}] of success.

Content:
So, the number of heads has the following probability mass function:

Content:
[MATH: f(x)|= ((5)/(x))((1)/(2))^{x}(1 − (1)/(2))^{5 − x}; = ((5)/(x))((1)/(2))^{x}((1)/(2))^{5 − x}; = ((5)/(x))((1)/(2))^{5}]

Content:
When a random variable [MATH: X] follows a binomial distribution consisting of [MATH: n] experiments (or trials) and the probability of success on each trial is [MATH: p,] we often write

Content:
[MATH: X\sim B(n,p).]

Content:
In words, we say, "the random variable [MATH: X] follows a binomial distribution with [MATH: n] trials and probability [MATH: p] of success on each trial."

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Random Variables that Follow a Binomial Distribution

Example Prompt:
Which of the following random variables could be modeled as a binomial distribution?

1. The ages of [MATH: 20] college professors
2. The number of questions answered correctly by a student in a [MATH: 12]-question exam
3. The heights of [MATH: 10] elementary school children

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A binomial distribution models the number of successes in a sequence of [MATH: n] independent experiments (where each outcome is either success or failure).

With that in mind, let's consider each of the given random variables.

- Random variable I could not be modeled as a binomial distribution. The ages cannot be interpreted as "success" or "failure."
- Random variable II could be modeled as a binomial distribution. The number of questions answered in a [MATH: 12]- question exam can be interpreted as the number of successes in a sequence of [MATH: 12] independent experiments.
- Random variable III could not be modeled as a binomial distribution. The heights cannot be interpreted as "success" or "failure."

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

---

3. The number of targets hit by an archer, out of [MATH: 10] targets total, if the archer has a [MATH: 30%] chance of hitting the target with any single shot.

Item 5 — Example: Computing the Probability of a Binomial Random Variable for Some Value

Example Prompt:
It is known that [MATH: 75\%] of students pass a particular exam. If [MATH: 5] students who took the exam are randomly selected, what is the probability that [MATH: 3] of them passed the exam? Round your answer to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let the random variable [MATH: X] be equal to the number of students that passed the exam.

Here, we have the following information:

- there are [MATH: n=5] students
- the probability that each student passed the exam is [MATH: p=75\%=0.75]

So, [MATH: X] follows a binomial distribution, where [MATH: X\sim B(5,0.75).] We want to find the probability that [MATH: x=3] of the students passed the exam.

The number of successes of a binomial random variable has the probability mass function

[MATH: P(X=x) = \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x},]

where [MATH: n] is the number of experiments, and [MATH: p] is the probability of success on each experiment.

Substituting the above information into the formula for probability mass function, we get

[MATH: P(X = 3)|= ((5)/(3))(0.75)^{3}(1 − 0.75)^{5 − 3}; = (5!)/(3!(5 − 3)!)(0.75)^{3}(0.25)^{2}; = 10(0.75)^{3}(0.25)^{2}; = 0.264]

rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

Item 8 — Example: Computing the Probability of a Binomial Random Variable Over an Interval

- the probability of rolling an even number on any roll of the die is

[MATH: P(X ≥ 7)|= P(X = 7) + P(X = 8); = ((8)/(7))(0.5)^{7}(0.5)^{8 − 7} + ((8)/(8))(0.5)^{8}(0.5)^{8 − 8}; = 8(0.5)^{7}(0.5) + 1(0.5)^{8}; = 0.035]
